allowed.description: true keeps the calls that were NOT refused (a failure counts as not refused — look at failed for those), false keeps the ones that were refused, rehearsed or stopped at the gate

refused.description: true keeps the calls a TOOL refused, false keeps the rest. A gate-level refusal (the call never reached the tool) and a rehearsal are not refusals

failed.description: true keeps the calls whose WORK failed (the tool answered with an error), false keeps the rest. A call the gate stopped is NOT a failure: the gate working is not something broken

post.description: [risk: read] Read this machine's gate trail: one line per tool call, with the arguments, whether the call did anything and why not. Use it when a call was REFUSED and there is nothing else to look up — a dangerous command refused for want of a confirmation never reaches the bastion, so the bastion's own audit has no record of it and this is the only one. It also answers 'which tools ran here recently', 'what failed here' (failed=true picks those out) and, most importantly, 'what may still be RUNNING on that machine?' — delivery=maybe_sent picks out the calls whose command may still be going, and delivery=not_sent the ones that never left this process (safe to run again). This is the local trail of attempted calls; the management plane's jms_command_audit is the bastion's log of what actually ran on the assets.

post.description: [risk: write] Collect the SAME set of facts from MANY machines and get back one matrix: a row per host, a column per fact. This is the fleet sweep -- disk, memory, service state, versions -- where the same questions are asked everywhere and the answers have to be lined up side by side. Each host gets ONE bastion session (so the facts of one host cannot mix with another's) and the hosts are swept in parallel. jmsx_exec_multi is the other way round: one command, many hosts. Pass dry_run=true first on a big sweep: it opens no session and reports how many rounds the sweep would take and roughly how many seconds it would cost, next to the risk classification.

post.description: [risk: write] Run a shell command on a JumpServer-managed machine THROUGH THE BASTION (koko 2222), returning stdout+stderr and the exit code. Use it for one command on one machine; jmsx_run runs several commands in one session, jmsx_exec_multi runs one command on many machines. The session is recorded in JumpServer's audit trail. The command runs as the asset account and is not elevated: prefix with 'sudo -n' for root. The answer names the account it ran as. Output is normally complete; with the koko terminal backend it is bounded by the terminal window, and full=true then fetches the rest (costs extra round trips).

post.description: [risk: write] Run the SAME command on several machines through the bastion and return each host's output. Use it when a fact has to be collected from a fleet (disk usage, a version, whether a service is up) and the answer must be per host: jms_job_run fans out too, but the v5 API exposes no execution output for a job, so this is the multi-host call that actually returns results. jmsx_collect_multi is the other way round: different facts per host. Hosts run in parallel, each in its own recorded bastion session, so ten hosts cost roughly two rounds instead of ten. A host that cannot be reached is reported as failed rather than aborting the run. Pass dry_run=true first on a big sweep: it opens no session and reports how many rounds the sweep would take and roughly how many seconds it would cost, next to the risk classification.

post.description: [risk: read] Download a whole REMOTE directory from an asset through the bastion, as one tar stream on the recorded session's channel, extracted here as it arrives — the mirror of jmsx_put_dir. Use it to pull back a config tree, a log bundle or an output directory in one call instead of hand-rolled tar|base64 over jmsx_exec or one jmsx_get_file per file. The semantics are MERGE: same-name files are overwritten, everything the destination already had is untouched. Extraction is defensive: an archive entry that is absolute or climbs out of the destination is skipped and counted in `skipped`, never written outside. Requires the connection-token path and tar on the asset.

post.description: [risk: read] Read a file FROM an asset through the bastion and return its content (base64-encoded over the wire, decoded for you). Pass offset and length to read only part of it: the window is applied on the remote side, so peeking at the head of a huge log costs only the bytes you asked for. A whole file is held in memory on this machine, so for a big one ask for a window rather than the lot. On the koko terminal path the answer is additionally bounded by the pane (a few dozen rows): larger files come back with truncated=true and the full size in available_bytes, so narrow the range server-side with head/sed/tail rather than assuming you saw everything.

post.description: [risk: destructive] Upload a whole LOCAL directory to an asset through the bastion, as one tar stream on the recorded session's channel. Use it to deploy a config tree, a script bundle or a small application directory in one call instead of one jmsx_put_file per file. The semantics are MERGE, not mirror: the archive extracts into the destination, overwriting same-name files and leaving everything the host already had alone — to make the remote tree exactly the local one, clear the destination first (jmsx_exec) and then upload. post.description: [risk: destructive] Upload a file to an asset through the bastion, over the same recorded session used for commands. Suitable for deploy scripts, config fragments and certificates. The file is written to a temporary name and renamed into place, so a transfer that fails halfway leaves the file that was there before untouched, and a symlinked destination keeps its link. The size is verified after the write, so a truncated transfer fails loudly instead of leaving a corrupt file behind. Content is base64, so nothing is interpreted by the shell. Supply the payload either as content (inline text), content_base64 (inline binary), or local_path (a file already on this machine) -- exactly one of them.（需确认：set confirm=true to write a file on the machine）

post.description: [risk: destructive] Copy a whole directory from one managed machine DIRECTLY to another through the bastion: the source's tar stream pipes straight into the destination's extractor, and the archive never lands on this machine — the directory form of jmsx_relay. Use it to push a config tree or a deployment bundle from one host to another without pulling it here and pushing it again. The semantics on the destination are MERGE (same-name files overwritten, entries it already had untouched). A straight-through stream carries no arrival proof — run a checksum on the destination (jmsx_exec) when the tree must be proven, or move it in two hops (jmsx_get_dir then jmsx_put_dir), which verifies with a sha256 manifest. Requires the connection-token path and tar on both machines.（需确认：set confirm=true to write files on the destination machine）
